4-axis-Cost-Benefit.card_intro: Connect total benefit, total cost, marginal benefit, marginal cost and net benefit across four linked panels.
4-axis-Cost-Benefit.card_prompt: Move the quantity q and explain why net benefit rises before MB = MC and falls afterwards.
4-axis-Cost-Benefit.intro_html: This graph presents the same choice in four equivalent ways. The top panels show total and marginal benefit and cost; the bottom panels show net benefit and the marginal change in net benefit. Move \(q\) and follow the same quantity across all four panels.
4-axis-Cost-Benefit.full_html:
What the four panels show

Suppose an agent chooses a quantity \(q\). Total benefit is \(B(q)\), total cost is \(C(q)\), and net benefit is

\[NB(q)=B(q)-C(q).\]

  • Top left: the vertical gap between total benefit and total cost is net benefit.
  • Top right: marginal benefit and marginal cost measure the effect of a small increase in quantity.
  • Bottom left: net benefit as a function of quantity.
  • Bottom right: marginal net benefit, which is the slope of the net-benefit curve.

Why the optimum occurs at MB = MC

Differentiating net benefit gives

\[NB'(q)=B'(q)-C'(q)=MB(q)-MC(q).\]

If \(MB(q)>MC(q)\), increasing quantity adds more benefit than cost, so net benefit rises. If \(MB(q)<MC(q)\), the next unit adds more cost than benefit, so net benefit falls. At an interior maximum,

\[NB'(q^*)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad MB(q^*)=MC(q^*).\]

This is not a separate rule imposed on the model. It is another way of saying that the net-benefit curve has reached a stationary point.

A worked observation from the default graph

The default functions are \(B(q)=0.7q\) and \(C(q)=0.1q^2\). Therefore \(MB=0.7\) and \(MC=0.2q\). Setting them equal gives \(q^*=3.5\). At that quantity,

\[NB(3.5)=0.7(3.5)-0.1(3.5)^2=1.225.\]

Move \(q\) slightly below and above 3.5. The sign of marginal net benefit should match the direction in which the net-benefit curve is moving.

Check your model

Do not confuse total and marginal objects. The height of \(B(q)\) is total benefit, while its slope is marginal benefit. The gap \(B(q)-C(q)\) is net benefit, while \(MB(q)-MC(q)\) is marginal net benefit.

Explore further: when is MB = MC not enough?

The condition \(MB=MC\) identifies a stationary point, not automatically a global maximum. With irregular functions there may be several intersections, or the best feasible choice may be at a boundary. In the default graph, net benefit is concave, so the intersection identifies the unique maximum.

Try increasing the fixed-cost parameter. This shifts total cost upward and net benefit downward, but it does not change marginal cost. The maximizing quantity can stay unchanged even though the maximum level of net benefit falls.

Elasticity-Flexible-Demand.card_intro: Use a power demand curve to see why elasticity can stay constant while price, quantity and slope change.
Elasticity-Flexible-Demand.card_prompt: Move the price marker, then change the exponent and identify which parameter controls elasticity.
Elasticity-Flexible-Demand.intro_html: The graph uses the power demand function \(Q_D(p)=Ap^{-B}\), where \(A>0\) and \(B>0\). It is designed to separate the position of a demand curve from its percentage responsiveness.
Elasticity-Flexible-Demand.full_html:
The main result

Point price elasticity is

\[E_D(p)=Q_D'(p)\frac{p}{Q_D(p)}.\]

Because \(Q_D'(p)=-ABp^{-B-1}\), substitution gives

\[E_D(p)=-B.\]

Price, quantity and slope all change as the marker moves, but elasticity does not. The exponent \(B\) fixes the elasticity everywhere on this curve.

What the two parameters do

The scale parameter \(A\) changes quantity demanded at every price without changing elasticity. The exponent \(B\) changes responsiveness: demand is elastic when \(B>1\), unit elastic when \(B=1\), and inelastic when \(0<B<1\).

Change one parameter at a time. If both move, it is easy to attribute a shift in the curve to the wrong mechanism.

How to use the graph

  1. Hold \(A\) and \(B\) fixed and move the price marker.
  2. Confirm that the elasticity readout remains \(-B\).
  3. Change \(A\) and observe that the curve moves but elasticity does not.
  4. Change \(B\) and classify demand using the magnitude of elasticity.

Check your model

Do not infer elasticity from steepness alone. Slope measures a unit change; elasticity combines slope with the price-to-quantity ratio. A curve whose slope changes can still have constant elasticity.

Explore further: elasticity and total expenditure

Total expenditure is \(pQ_D(p)=Ap^{1-B}\). It rises with price when \(B<1\), is unchanged when \(B=1\), and falls with price when \(B>1\). The usual total-revenue test follows directly from the same exponent that determines elasticity.

Elasticity-Staircase-Demand.card_intro: Explore elasticity when quantity changes in discrete jumps rather than along a smooth demand curve.
Elasticity-Staircase-Demand.card_prompt: Move price across a threshold and decide whether point or midpoint elasticity is the meaningful measure.
Elasticity-Staircase-Demand.intro_html: This graph uses a staircase demand schedule. Quantity can remain unchanged over an interval of prices and then jump when a reservation-price threshold is crossed. It shows exactly where a derivative-based elasticity is informative—and where it is not.
Elasticity-Staircase-Demand.full_html:
Local responses and jumps

For a differentiable demand curve, point elasticity is \(E_D(p)=Q_D'(p)p/Q_D(p)\). On a flat step, quantity is locally constant, so the local price response is zero. At a jump price the derivative does not exist, so point elasticity is not defined.

This does not make the jump economically unimportant. It means that a local derivative is the wrong summary for a finite change across the threshold.

Use midpoint elasticity for a finite movement

For a movement from \((p_1,Q_1)\) to \((p_2,Q_2)\), use

\[E_D^{mid}=\frac{(Q_2-Q_1)/[(Q_1+Q_2)/2]}{(p_2-p_1)/[(p_1+p_2)/2]}.\]

The midpoint denominators make the reported percentage change independent of which observation is called the starting point.

How to use the graph

First place the price marker within one step and make a very small price change. Then move the marker across a threshold and compare the finite change in quantity. State which experiment you are describing before quoting an elasticity.

Check your model

“Elasticity is zero” is correct only for a local movement inside a step. It is not a description of a movement that crosses a jump. Also, “undefined at the threshold” does not mean “no response”; it means the point-elasticity formula has no derivative to use.

Explore further: why staircase demand becomes smoother in large markets

Each individual buyer can create a discrete jump. When many buyers with different reservation prices are horizontally aggregated, the jumps become smaller relative to total market quantity. A smooth demand curve is often an approximation to this finely stepped market schedule.

Market-interventions-revised.card_intro: Compare taxes, subsidies, price floors, price support and quantity restrictions against the competitive benchmark.
Market-interventions-revised.card_prompt: Select a policy, identify the buyer and seller prices, then account for quantity, surplus and government activity.
Market-interventions-revised.intro_html: This graph puts the main market interventions on the same supply-and-demand diagram. Begin with the competitive equilibrium, then change one policy control at a time. Taxes, subsidies, price floors, price support and quotas are core course material; voluntary reduction is included as an optional comparison.
Market-interventions-revised.full_html:
Start from the competitive benchmark

Without intervention, the demand price equals the supply price at the traded quantity. The units to the left of equilibrium create gains from trade because willingness to pay is at least marginal cost. An intervention changes a price, a quantity, or the wedge between what buyers pay and sellers receive.

Taxes and subsidies

A per-unit tax creates a wedge:

\[P_b-P_s=t.\]

The buyer price rises, the seller price falls and trade contracts. Statutory incidence—who sends the tax to government—does not determine economic incidence. The more inelastic side changes quantity less and typically bears more of the burden. Tax revenue is \(tQ_t\); the lost gains from the trades that no longer occur form deadweight loss.

A subsidy creates the opposite wedge and expands trade. Government expenditure is the per-unit subsidy multiplied by the subsidised quantity. If the competitive quantity was already efficient, the extra trades cost more than buyers value them at the margin.

Price floors and government price support

A binding price floor lies above equilibrium. With no government purchase, sellers wish to supply more than buyers demand, so the short side of the market determines trade. The unsold surplus is not consumer or producer surplus.

Under price support, government purchases some or all of the excess supply to maintain the target price. This changes both production and the fiscal account. Record private consumption, total production, government purchases and expenditure separately.

Quotas and quantity restrictions

A binding quota fixes trade below the competitive quantity. The gap between demand and supply prices at that quantity is a quota rent:

\[\text{quota rent per unit}=P_b-P_s.\]

Who receives that rent depends on who owns or is allocated the quota rights. A quota can therefore have the same quantity as a tax while distributing surplus differently.

How to use the graph

  1. Record the original equilibrium price, quantity and total surplus.
  2. Turn on one intervention and decide whether it binds.
  3. Identify buyer price, seller price, quantity traded, and government revenue or expenditure.
  4. Only then compare consumer surplus, producer surplus, rents, fiscal effects and deadweight loss.

Check your model

A higher observed price is not by itself a welfare conclusion. Transfers between consumers, producers, quota owners and government must not be counted as lost surplus. Deadweight loss comes from mutually beneficial trades that are prevented, or inefficient trades and production that are induced.

Explore further: voluntary reduction

Voluntary reduction can reproduce the quantity of a formal restriction only if participants actually coordinate on the lower output or purchase level. Each participant may prefer others to reduce while continuing themselves, so enforcement and free-riding become central. The graph shows the price-and-quantity comparison; it does not solve that strategic incentive problem.

Lectorial.card_intro: A local council chooses the scale of a habitat-restoration project using numerical benefit and cost functions.
Lectorial.card_prompt: Find the project scale H that maximises net benefit and calculate the resulting benefit, cost and net benefit.
Lectorial.intro_html:
The Riverton Council is deciding how many hectares, \(H\), to restore. All monetary values are measured in thousands of dollars. The council estimates total benefit and total cost as

\[B(H)=654H-40H^2,\qquad C(H)=110H+40H^2,\qquad H\ge 0.\]

Use the graph to estimate the best project scale before solving the problem algebraically.
Lectorial.full_html:
Question

  1. Calculate total benefit, total cost and net benefit when \(H=0\), \(H=3.4\) and \(H=5\).
  2. Derive \(NB(H)\), \(MB(H)\) and \(MC(H)\). Use \(MB(H)=MC(H)\) to find the optimal number of hectares.
  3. At the optimum, report total benefit, total cost and net benefit. Explain why restoring more land beyond this point lowers net benefit.
Lectorial.answer_html:
Show the worked solution

The requested values are:

At \(H=0\), \(B=0\), \(C=0\) and \(NB=0\).

At \(H=3.4\), \(B=1761.2\), \(C=836.4\) and \(NB=924.8\).

At \(H=5\), \(B=2270\), \(C=1550\) and \(NB=720\).

Net benefit is

\[NB(H)=654H-40H^2-(110H+40H^2)=544H-80H^2.\]

The marginal functions are

\[MB(H)=654-80H,\qquad MC(H)=110+80H.\]

Set marginal benefit equal to marginal cost:

\[654-80H=110+80H\quad\Longrightarrow\quad H^*=3.4.\]

All monetary values are in thousands of dollars. Since \(NB''(H)=-160<0\), the stationary point is a maximum. For \(H>3.4\), marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit, so expanding the project lowers net benefit.

Max.card_intro: A food-safety authority chooses how many inspection teams to use when inspections reduce expected harm but cost money.
Max.card_prompt: Using H(x)=32/(x+1) and C(x)=2x, find the inspection level that minimises total expected loss.
Max.intro_html:
A food-safety authority can deploy \(x\) inspection teams. Without inspection, expected harm is 32 units. With \(x\) teams, expected harm and inspection cost are

\[H(x)=\frac{32}{x+1},\qquad C(x)=2x,\qquad x\ge 0.\]

The graph treats \(x\) as continuous. In this example the calculated optimum is also a whole number of teams.
Max.full_html:
Question

  1. Calculate expected harm, inspection cost and total loss when \(x=0,1,3\) and \(7\).
  2. Write \(L(x)=H(x)+C(x)\). Use \(MB(x)=-H'(x)\) and \(MC(x)=2\) to find the value of \(x\) that minimises total loss.
  3. Calculate harm, inspection cost and total loss at the optimum. Compare it with the loss of 32 when \(x=0\), and explain why total loss eventually rises.
Max.answer_html:
Show the worked solution

Total expected loss is

\[L(x)=\frac{32}{x+1}+2x.\]

The requested values are:

At \(x=0\), \((H,C,L)=(32,0,32)\).

At \(x=1\), \((H,C,L)=(16,2,18)\).

At \(x=3\), \((H,C,L)=(8,6,14)\).

At \(x=7\), \((H,C,L)=(4,14,18)\).

The marginal benefit of inspection is the negative of marginal harm:

\[MB(x)=-H'(x)=\frac{32}{(x+1)^2},\qquad MC(x)=2.\]

Set the two marginal values equal:

\[\frac{32}{(x+1)^2}=2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad (x+1)^2=16\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^*=3.\]

With no inspection, \(L(0)=32\). The three-team policy reduces total expected loss by 18 units. Also, \(L''(x)=64/(x+1)^3>0\), so this stationary point is a minimum. For \(x>3\), marginal benefit is below marginal cost, so each additional team costs more than the harm it removes and total loss rises.

W1Quiz.card_intro: Three short numerical problems review partial derivatives, a nonlinear system and a logarithmic derivative.
W1Quiz.card_prompt: Calculate the farm's output and marginal products, solve the positive nonlinear system, and evaluate the logarithmic function at 10.
W1Quiz.intro_html: This review contains the three numerical setups already shown in the Desmos graph. Work through each calculation before checking the plotted answer.
W1Quiz.full_html:
Question 1: production

For \(Q(K,L)=K^{\alpha}L^{\beta}\), let \(\alpha=1\), \(\beta=2\) and \((K,L)=(2,2)\). Calculate output, \(MP_K\) and \(MP_L\).

Question 2: nonlinear system

Find the positive values of \(x\) and \(y\) that satisfy \(y^2/x^3=1/4\) and \(4x+5y=36\). Check your answer in both equations.

Question 3: logarithms

For \(g(t)=5\ln t\), calculate \(g(10)\), derive \(g'(t)\), and interpret \(g'(10)\).
W1Quiz.answer_html:
Show the worked solutions

Question 1

At the stated values,

\[Q(2,2)=2^1\times2^2=8.\]

The marginal products are

\[MP_K=\alpha K^{\alpha-1}L^{\beta},\qquad MP_L=\beta K^{\alpha}L^{\beta-1}.\]

Therefore \(MP_K(2,2)=4\) and \(MP_L(2,2)=8\).

Question 2

Because quantities are positive, the nonlinear condition gives \(y=\tfrac12x^{3/2}\). Substituting into the second equation yields

\[4x+\frac52x^{3/2}=36.\]

The positive solution is \(x=4\), which gives \(y=4\). The checks are \(4(4)+5(4)=36\) and \(4^2/4^3=1/4\).

Question 3

\[g(10)=5\ln(10)\approx11.513,\qquad g'(t)=\frac5t,\qquad g'(10)=0.5.\]

At \(t=10\), the score is increasing at an instantaneous rate of 0.5 points per hour. For a small change \(\Delta t\), the corresponding change in the score is approximately \(0.5\Delta t\) points.

Elasticity.card_intro: Connect slope, percentage responsiveness and total expenditure along linear demand and supply curves.
Elasticity.card_prompt: Move the price marker along linear demand and explain why elasticity changes although slope does not.
Elasticity.intro_html: The graph begins with linear demand \(Q_D(p)=A-Bp\) and then adds supply. The derivative is constant, but elasticity is not, because elasticity measures percentage rather than unit changes.
Elasticity.full_html:
Slope is not elasticity

Demand elasticity is

\[E_D(p)=Q_D'(p)\frac{p}{Q_D(p)}=-B\frac{p}{A-Bp}.\]

The slope term \(-B\) is constant. The price-to-quantity ratio is not. Near the quantity intercept demand is inelastic; at the midpoint its elasticity has magnitude one; near the choke price its magnitude becomes large.

Reading percentage responsiveness

If the magnitude of demand elasticity is greater than one, a 1 percent price increase produces a greater than 1 percent quantity decrease. If it is less than one, the quantity response is proportionally smaller. Demand elasticity is negative under the usual law of demand, although discussions often report its magnitude.

Supply elasticity uses the same logic, \(E_S(p)=Q_S'(p)p/Q_S(p)\), and is normally positive.

How to use the graph

  1. Hold the demand curve fixed and move the point from the quantity intercept toward the choke price.
  2. Locate the midpoint and verify unit elasticity.
  3. Compare the sign and magnitude of the elasticity with the direction of total expenditure \(pQ\).
  4. For a large finite change, use the midpoint formula rather than a one-sided percentage change.

Check your model

“A steeper curve is less elastic” is safe only when comparing curves at the same price and quantity. Along one straight-line demand curve, slope is constant while elasticity changes from zero in magnitude to arbitrarily large.

Explore further: elasticity and total expenditure

When demand is elastic, a small price increase lowers total expenditure because the percentage fall in quantity is larger. When demand is inelastic, the same price increase raises total expenditure. At unit elasticity the two percentage changes offset locally.

Consumers-Problem.card_intro: Build the consumer's problem from preferences, the budget set and the highest attainable indifference curve.
Consumers-Problem.card_prompt: Switch preference types and decide whether tangency, a corner or a kink determines the optimum.
Consumers-Problem.intro_html: The consumer chooses the most preferred bundle among those that are affordable. The graph lets you separate the two ingredients of the problem: prices and income determine the feasible set, while preferences rank the bundles inside it.
Consumers-Problem.full_html:
The constrained choice problem

The budget set is

\[p_xx+p_yy\le I.\]

With monotonic preferences, the chosen bundle lies on the budget line because an affordable increase in at least one good would be preferred. The consumer then reaches the highest indifference curve that still touches the feasible set.

When tangency works

At a smooth interior optimum,

\[MRS_{xy}=\frac{MU_x}{MU_y}=\frac{p_x}{p_y}.\]

The left side is the consumer's willingness to trade \(y\) for \(x\); the right side is the market trade-off. If they differ, the consumer can normally rearrange spending and reach a preferred affordable bundle.

When tangency does not work

The equation is not a universal recipe. Perfect substitutes can produce a corner, perfect complements are optimised at a kink, and a smooth utility function can still have a boundary solution. A first-order condition generates a candidate; feasibility and a comparison with relevant corners determine the solution.

How to use the graph

When a control moves, first classify it. A change in income shifts the budget line in parallel. A change in one price rotates it. A change in a utility parameter alters preferences rather than affordability. Then inspect whether the proposed optimum is a tangency, kink or corner.

Check your model

The consumer does not maximise the utility number in the abstract. Utility ranks feasible bundles. A strictly increasing transformation can change every displayed number while leaving indifference curves and choices unchanged.

Explore further: what assumptions make the picture well behaved?

Completeness and transitivity give a consistent ranking. Monotonicity pushes the choice to the budget boundary. Convexity makes averages attractive and helps make a tangency a maximum rather than a minimum. If one of these assumptions fails, the familiar diagram can change substantially.

Indifference-curve.card_intro: Read indifference curves as preference contours and connect their slope to the marginal rate of substitution.
Indifference-curve.card_prompt: Move the reference bundle, compare the two utility specifications and explain what the slope means locally.
Indifference-curve.intro_html: An indifference curve collects all bundles that the consumer ranks equally. Its location represents a utility level; its local slope represents a willingness to trade. Those are different objects and should not be read interchangeably.
Indifference-curve.full_html:
Slope and the marginal rate of substitution

Holding utility constant gives

\[\frac{dy}{dx}\bigg|_{u=\bar u}=-\frac{MU_x}{MU_y}=-MRS_{xy}.\]

The minus sign is the geometric slope. The positive ratio \(MU_x/MU_y\) is usually reported as the amount of \(y\) the consumer is willing to give up for an additional unit of \(x\).

Convexity and diminishing MRS

For standard Cobb–Douglas preferences, indifference curves are downward sloping and convex. As the consumer acquires more \(x\) and less \(y\) along one curve, the willingness to sacrifice \(y\) for still more \(x\) falls. Convexity is about the ranking of mixtures, not simply whether a curve looks curved.

How to use the graph

Move the reference bundle and note that the graph selects a different utility level. Then keep the bundle fixed and change the utility specification. Compare the local slope and curvature rather than comparing raw utility numbers across specifications.

Check your model

An indifference curve alone cannot prove that a good is inferior. Inferiority is an income response of demand: after solving the constrained problem, the quantity demanded must fall as income rises with prices fixed. The Week 3 inferior-good graph performs that comparison.

Explore further: why utility transformations do not change choice

If \(v(x,y)=f(u(x,y))\) and \(f\) is strictly increasing, \(v\) assigns different numbers but preserves every ranking. Its marginal utilities change, yet their ratio—and therefore the MRS—remains the same.

Utility-Max.card_intro: View indifference curves as level curves of a utility surface and utility maximisation as the highest feasible point.
Utility-Max.card_prompt: Rotate the graph, move a bundle along the budget line and connect its 3D height to the 2D indifference map.
Utility-Max.intro_html: This optional graph connects the familiar two-dimensional consumer-choice diagram to the three-dimensional utility surface behind it. A bundle \((x,y)\) lies on the floor; its height \(z=u(x,y)\) records its utility ranking.
Utility-Max.full_html:
From bundles to a utility surface

The horizontal axes measure \(x\) and \(y\). The vertical axis records

\[z=u(x,y)=x^ay^b.\]

Fixing utility at \(\bar u\) cuts the surface with a horizontal plane. Project that intersection onto the floor and the ordinary two-dimensional indifference curve appears.

How to explore the graph

  1. Rotate the graph until both the floor and surface are visible.
  2. Move the bundle and follow its vertical segment to the surface.
  3. Turn on an indifference curve and move along it. Quantities change but height remains fixed.
  4. Turn on the budget-line folders and move along the feasible path on the surface.

Utility maximisation on the surface

The budget boundary is \(y=I/p_y-(p_x/p_y)x\). Lifting it onto the surface produces the feasible utility path

\[z=u\!\left(x,\frac{I}{p_y}-\frac{p_x}{p_y}x\right).\]

The consumer chooses the highest point on that path. Viewed from above, it is the point where the highest attainable indifference curve touches the budget line.

A worked observation from the default graph

With \(a=b=1\), \(p_x=p_y=5\) and \(I=15\), the budget is \(x+y=3\). Along it,

\[u(x,3-x)=x(3-x),\]

which is maximised at \((x^*,y^*)=(1.5,1.5)\), with utility 2.25 and \(MRS=p_x/p_y=1\).

Check your model

Vertical distance is not a measurable difference in happiness. Utility is ordinal. Also, utility is constant while moving along one indifference curve; the optimum lies on the highest curve the budget allows the consumer to reach.

Explore further: why the 2D graph is usually enough

Consumer choice depends on the ranking of feasible bundles, and a contour map preserves that ranking while making the budget comparison easier. The 3D surface is useful for intuition, but routine analysis normally uses its two-dimensional level curves.

The smooth tangency shown here can be replaced by a corner or kink under other preferences.

Discrete-Demand-Supply.card_intro: Construct market demand and supply from individual bids and asks, producing staircase curves and discrete trades.
Discrete-Demand-Supply.card_prompt: Change the number of traders or add a unit tax, then identify the last trade that still creates surplus.
Discrete-Demand-Supply.intro_html: Each buyer has a willingness to pay and each seller has a willingness to accept. Sorting those values creates staircase demand and supply schedules. The market outcome can then be read one possible trade at a time.
Discrete-Demand-Supply.full_html:
From individual values to market curves

Rank buyers from highest to lowest willingness to pay and sellers from lowest to highest opportunity cost. The \(k\)th trade creates gains when

\[WTP_k\ge WTA_k.\]

Continue until the next buyer values the unit less than the next seller's cost. The efficient quantity is the number of mutually beneficial trades.

Price and surplus in a discrete market

With step curves, the competitive price need not be a single number. Any price between the marginal successful buyer's value and seller's cost can support the same quantity, depending on the trading institution. Total surplus is

\[TS=\sum_{k\in\text{completed trades}}(WTP_k-WTA_k).\]

Taxes and market size

A unit tax can be represented by lowering buyers' net bids or raising sellers' effective asks. Either representation creates the same wedge and may eliminate marginal trades. Increasing the number of heterogeneous traders adds more steps and can make the market schedule look smoother.

How to use the graph

Do not begin by searching for a geometric intersection. Pair the highest remaining bid with the lowest remaining ask, decide whether that trade creates surplus, and proceed sequentially. Then check that the staircase diagram records the same marginal trade.

Check your model

Equality is not required for a trade to be efficient. When \(WTP_k>WTA_k\), the difference is a gain from trade that can be divided between buyer and seller through the price.

Explore further: what determines a price inside the interval?

The supply-and-demand schedules determine which trades can create surplus, but a bargaining rule, auction protocol or posted-price institution can determine how that surplus is divided. This is why the same efficient quantity can coexist with a range of transaction prices in a small discrete market.

Budget-Line-With-Complex-Pricing.card_intro: Maya faces a bulk discount: the first 20 data packs cost $2 each and every later pack costs $1.
Budget-Line-With-Complex-Pricing.card_prompt: With income $51.30 and u(x,y)=x^1.2y, derive the kinked budget line and find Maya's optimal bundle.
Budget-Line-With-Complex-Pricing.intro_html:
Maya allocates a weekly budget of $51.30 between mobile-data packs \(x\) and a composite good \(y\). Each unit of \(y\) costs $1. Her provider charges $2 for each of the first 20 data packs and $1 for each pack after the twentieth. Maya's preferences are represented by

\[u(x,y)=x^{1.2}y.\]
Budget-Line-With-Complex-Pricing.full_html:
Question

  1. Calculate Maya's data spending and the amount left for \(y\) when she buys 12, 20 and 27 packs. Then write one budget equation using \(\min\{x,20\}\) and \(\max\{x-20,0\}\).
  2. Write the budget line separately for \(0\le x\le20\) and \(x\ge20\). Find the two intercepts and the kink, then draw the budget line.
  3. Find Maya's best bundle on each section. Check whether each candidate belongs to that section, then compare the valid candidates with the kink \((20,11.30)\) and state her optimal bundle.
Budget-Line-With-Complex-Pricing.answer_html:
Show the worked solution

The complete budget equation is

\[2\min\{x,20\}+\max\{x-20,0\}+y=51.3.\]

When \(x=12\), data spending is $24 and \(y=27.30\). When \(x=20\), data spending is $40 and \(y=11.30\). When \(x=27\), data spending is $47 and \(y=4.30\).

The two budget segments are

\[2x+y=51.3\quad(0\le x\le20),\]

\[40+(x-20)+y=51.3\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x+y=31.3\quad(x\ge20).\]

The intercepts are \((0,51.3)\) and \((31.3,0)\). The kink is \((20,11.3)\).

For \(u=x^{1.2}y\), the expenditure share on \(x\) is \(1.2/2.2\). On the first segment,

\[x_1=\frac{1.2}{2.2}\frac{51.3}{2}\approx13.99,\qquad y_1=51.3-2x_1\approx23.32.\]

This candidate is valid because \(13.99<20\).

On the second segment, the adjusted budget is \(x+y=31.3\), so its unconstrained Cobb–Douglas candidate is

\[x_2=\frac{1.2}{2.2}(31.3)\approx17.07.\]

This candidate is invalid because it does not satisfy \(x\ge20\). The best point on the second segment is therefore the kink \((20,11.3)\).

Utility at the valid first-segment candidate is approximately \(552.98\), compared with \(411.45\) at the kink. The two feasible corners give zero utility. Maya therefore chooses approximately

\[(x^*,y^*)=(13.99,23.32).\]

Consumers-Problem-Lecture-Example.card_intro: Alex allocates a $69 weekly budget between meals priced at $9 and study-resource bundles priced at $12.
Consumers-Problem-Lecture-Example.card_prompt: Find Alex's utility-maximising bundle subject to 9x+12y=69, then verify the budget and tangency conditions.
Consumers-Problem-Lecture-Example.intro_html:
Alex has $69 per week to spend on meals \(x\) and study-resource bundles \(y\). A meal costs $9 and a study bundle costs $12. Alex's preferences are represented by

\[u(x,y)=x^{1/3}y.\]
Consumers-Problem-Lecture-Example.full_html:
Question

Determine the utility-maximising bundle \((x^*,y^*)\) that Alex can afford. Use the budget line and tangency condition, then verify the result.

  1. Write Alex's budget equation \(9x+12y=69\). Calculate its two intercepts and its slope, then draw it on the graph.
  2. For \(u(x,y)=x^{1/3}y\), derive \(MRS_{xy}\). Use \(MRS_{xy}=9/12\) together with the budget equation to find Alex's optimal bundle.
  3. Calculate how many dollars Alex spends on each good and check that total expenditure is exactly $69. Confirm that the bundle matches the tangency shown in Desmos.
Consumers-Problem-Lecture-Example.answer_html:
Show the worked solution

The budget is

\[9x+12y=69,\qquad \text{slope}=-\frac{9}{12}=-\frac34.\]

The intercepts are \((23/3,0)\approx(7.667,0)\) and \((0,23/4)=(0,5.75)\).

Marginal utilities imply

\[MRS_{xy}=\frac{MU_x}{MU_y}=\frac{y}{3x}.\]

At an interior optimum,

\[\frac{y}{3x}=\frac{9}{12}=\frac34\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=\frac94x.\]

Substituting into the budget gives

\[9x+12\left(\frac94x\right)=69\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 36x=69.\]

Therefore

\[x^*=\frac{23}{12}\approx1.917,\qquad y^*=\frac{69}{16}=4.3125.\]

Alex spends $17.25 on meals because \(9x^*=17.25\), and $51.75 on study-resource bundles because \(12y^*=51.75\). Thus total expenditure is $69.

Finally, \(MRS_{xy}=y^*/(3x^*)=3/4=9/12\), so the bundle satisfies the tangency condition shown in Desmos.

Inferior-Good.card_intro: Trace an income-consumption path where demand for x falls as income rises, while checking local and global optima.
Inferior-Good.card_prompt: Raise income, follow the orange path up and left, and compare the larger-root interior candidate with the corner.
Inferior-Good.intro_html: This graph is deliberately trickier than the standard consumer problem. The utility function can produce two stationary points on a budget line, and the first-order condition alone does not identify the optimum. The orange curve traces the selected income-consumption path: over the relevant range it moves upward and left as income rises, so demand for \(x\) falls.
Inferior-Good.full_html:
The model

Preferences are represented by

\[u(x,y)=a\ln x+\frac{y^2}{2},\]

subject to \(p_xx+p_yy=I\). The marginal-rate condition for an interior stationary point is

\[\frac{a}{xy}=\frac{p_x}{p_y}.\]

Combining this condition with the budget gives

\[y^2-\frac{I}{p_y}y+a=0.\]

Two stationary points are not two maxima

Interior stationary bundles exist only when the quadratic discriminant is non-negative. When there are two positive roots, the smaller-\(y\) root is a local minimum of utility along the budget line, while the larger-\(y\) root is a local maximum. Because the objective is not globally concave, the larger-root candidate must still be compared with the feasible corner \((I/p_x,0)\).

Why x is inferior on the selected branch

At an interior stationary point,

\[x=\frac{ap_y}{p_xy}.\]

Along the larger-root branch, a rise in income raises \(y\). The expression above then makes \(x\) fall. This is exactly what the orange income-consumption curve shows when it moves up and left.

How to use the graph

  1. Hold prices fixed and raise income.
  2. Track both stationary candidates rather than assuming every tangency is optimal.
  3. Compare utility at the larger-root candidate with the corner.
  4. Only after the global choice is identified should the orange path be interpreted as demand.

Check your model

Inferior does not mean “bad,” and it does not mean demand slopes upward in own price. A good is inferior when its demand falls as income rises, holding prices fixed. The classification applies to the demand function over a range, not to an isolated indifference curve.

Explore further: inferior is not the same as Giffen

A Giffen good has an upward-sloping ordinary own-price demand over some range. That requires a negative income effect strong enough to outweigh the substitution effect. Inferiority is necessary for that mechanism but not sufficient. This graph establishes an income response; it does not by itself establish Giffen behaviour.

The example also shows why convexity matters. With standard convex preferences, a valid interior tangency is normally a maximum. Here the non-concavity makes a global utility comparison essential.

Perfect-Complements.card_intro: Solve a fixed-proportions consumer problem where the optimum occurs at a kink rather than a smooth tangency.
Perfect-Complements.card_prompt: Change prices or income and verify that the chosen bundle remains on the fixed-proportion ray.
Perfect-Complements.intro_html: Perfect complements are consumed in a fixed effective proportion. Extra units of only one good do not raise utility once the other good is the limiting input, so the usual smooth tangency condition is not available.
Perfect-Complements.full_html:
The kink condition

For

\[u(x,y)=\min\{ax,by\},\]

an efficient bundle satisfies \(ax=by\). If the budget also binds, the optimal demands are

\[x^*=\frac{bI}{bp_x+ap_y},\qquad y^*=\frac{aI}{bp_x+ap_y}.\]

Why there is no substitution along an indifference curve

At the kink, the indifference curve has no single slope. Moving away from the fixed-proportion ray creates excess units of one good without increasing the minimum. Price changes alter how much of the composite bundle the consumer can afford, but they do not produce the smooth substitution response seen with Cobb–Douglas preferences.

How to use the graph

First identify the kink ray. Then change income and confirm that the optimum moves outward along that ray. Change one price and observe that both quantities adjust because the cost of one complete fixed-proportion bundle has changed.

Check your model

Do not force \(MRS=p_x/p_y\) at the kink. The correct method is to combine the fixed-proportion condition with the budget equation.

Explore further: perfect complements as a limiting case

CES preferences approach perfect complements as substitutability becomes very low. In the limit, compensated substitution between the goods disappears and the smooth indifference curves become L-shaped.

Quasi-Linear-Optimization.card_intro: Solve a quasilinear consumer problem and identify the special income effect at an interior solution.
Quasi-Linear-Optimization.card_prompt: Change income and verify which demand stays fixed until a corner is reached.
Quasi-Linear-Optimization.intro_html: The graph uses \(u(x,y)=x+\sqrt y\) and \(p_xx+p_yy=I\). Utility is linear in \(x\) and curved in \(y\), producing a particularly useful demand pattern.
Quasi-Linear-Optimization.full_html:
The interior solution

At a smooth interior optimum,

\[\frac{MU_x}{MU_y}=2\sqrt y=\frac{p_x}{p_y}.\]

Hence

\[y^*=\left(\frac{p_x}{2p_y}\right)^2,\qquad x^*=\frac{I}{p_x}-\frac{p_x}{4p_y}.\]

The special income response

At the interior solution, demand for \(y\) depends on prices but not income. Once the preferred amount of \(y\) is purchased, additional income is spent entirely on \(x\). This is the zero-income-effect property often used in quasilinear models.

Where the formula stops working

The interior formula requires enough income to afford \(y^*\). If income is too low, the calculated \(x^*\) is negative. That is a signal to return to the constrained problem: the solution is a corner with \(x=0\), not a negative quantity.

How to use the graph

Raise income gradually. While the solution is interior, the optimum should move horizontally: \(y\) stays fixed and \(x\) rises. Then lower income until the corner appears and note precisely where the zero-income-effect conclusion ceases to apply.

Check your model

“Quasilinear demand has no income effect” is too broad. One good has zero income effect only in the interior region. Corners restore an income response.

Revealed-Preference.card_intro: Infer preference comparisons from observed choices and the budget sets that made alternatives affordable.
Revealed-Preference.card_prompt: Step through the observations and shade only the comparisons justified by actual affordability.
Revealed-Preference.intro_html: Revealed preference begins with observed choices rather than a stated utility function. A chosen bundle tells us something about rejected bundles only when those alternatives were actually affordable at the time.
Revealed-Preference.full_html:
Direct revealed preference

If \(A\) is chosen from a budget set that also contains \(B\), then \(A\) is directly revealed weakly preferred to \(B\). If \(B\) lay outside the budget, the observation gives no comparison between them.

Chains and consistency

If \(A\) is revealed preferred to \(B\) and \(B\) to \(C\), transitivity supports an indirect ranking of \(A\) above \(C\). A later choice can contradict the ranking if it selects \(B\) while \(A\) is affordable under the relevant strict conditions.

How to use the graph

  1. Identify the chosen bundle in each observation.
  2. Shade the budget set that was available.
  3. Compare the choice only with bundles inside that set.
  4. Use the rollout control to distinguish direct observations from conclusions that require transitivity.

Check your model

A budget line is not just background geometry. Without affordability, there is no revealed comparison. Also, weak revealed preference does not mean the consumer is indifferent; the chosen bundle may be strictly preferred.

Explore further: what can choice data fail to reveal?

Finite observations generally leave many rankings unresolved. Revealed-preference tests can identify contradictions with stable utility maximisation, but passing the tests does not uniquely recover the consumer's utility function. The data reveal only the comparisons supported by observed opportunities and choices.

Utility-Max-CES.card_intro: Use CES preferences to vary substitutability continuously between near-complements and near-substitutes.
Utility-Max-CES.card_prompt: Move the curvature and price controls, then track the indifference curves and the optimal marker A.
Utility-Max-CES.intro_html: The graph uses a constant-elasticity-of-substitution utility function of the form \(u=[(ax)^r+(by)^r]^{1/r}\). The curvature parameter changes how readily the consumer substitutes between the goods; the price controls move both the budget line and the displayed optimum.
Utility-Max-CES.full_html:
Curvature and substitution

For the standard CES form, the elasticity of substitution is

\[\sigma=\frac{1}{1-r}.\]

As \(r\) approaches one, the goods become close substitutes. As \(r\) becomes very negative, they become close complements. Intermediate values produce smooth, convex indifference curves.

The optimum

At a smooth interior optimum, the MRS equals the price ratio. Increasing \(p_1\) or \(p_2\) rotates the budget line, so the marker \(A\) should move. Its response depends on both the new market trade-off and the curvature of preferences.

How to use the graph

  1. Choose a middle value of \(r\) and move each price separately.
  2. Watch the budget rotation and verify that marker \(A\) remains on the budget line.
  3. Move \(r\) toward the complement and substitute limits.
  4. Compare how strongly the optimal ratio of goods responds to the same relative-price change.

Check your model

The elasticity of substitution is not the price elasticity of demand. It describes how the chosen input or consumption ratio responds to a change in the MRS or relative price while remaining on an indifference curve.

Explore further: the limiting cases

At the perfect-substitutes limit, a small relative-price change can switch the optimum between corners. At the perfect-complements limit, the optimum remains on a kink ray and compensated substitution disappears. These limits are useful precisely because the smooth tangency formula eventually stops being the right tool.

Sales-vs-Income-Tax.card_intro: Compare a tax on one good with an income tax that raises the same revenue, then separate substitution and income effects.
Sales-vs-Income-Tax.card_prompt: Match revenue, compare the two budget sets and explain why equal revenue need not mean equal utility.
Sales-vs-Income-Tax.intro_html: A sales tax on one good changes its relative price and rotates the budget line. An income tax reduces purchasing power while leaving the relative-price slope unchanged. Matching government revenue makes the behavioural difference visible.
Sales-vs-Income-Tax.full_html:
Two taxes, two budget changes

A sales tax combines a substitution effect with an income effect: the taxed good becomes relatively more expensive and purchasing power falls. An income tax shifts the budget line inward in parallel, creating a purchasing-power effect without the same distortion in the relative price between the two goods.

Why revenue equivalence is not utility equivalence

In the standard consumer model, a revenue-equivalent income tax generally leaves the consumer at least as well off as the tax on one good. The consumer can still choose a bundle with the preferred market trade-off rather than being pushed away by a commodity-specific wedge. This statement holds within the graph's assumptions; administrative, labour-supply and distributional effects are outside it.

Hicksian and Slutsky compensation

Hicksian compensation restores the original utility level at the new prices. Slutsky compensation supplies enough income to make the original bundle affordable at the new prices. They answer different counterfactual questions, differ for a finite price change, and coincide only to first order for a very small change.

How to use the graph

  1. Record the untaxed optimum.
  2. Apply the sales tax and calculate its revenue at the new quantity.
  3. Set the income tax to collect the same amount.
  4. Compare budget slopes, chosen bundles and utility—not only one coordinate.

Check your model

Equal tax rates, equal revenue and equal consumer burden are three different comparisons. State which one is being held fixed before drawing a welfare conclusion.

Explore further: when might the policy ranking change?

A broad income tax can affect labour supply, evasion and distribution, while a targeted commodity tax may address an externality or information problem. Those mechanisms can reverse a simple consumer-only ranking. The graph isolates one point: holding revenue fixed, changing a relative price adds a distortion that a lump-sum purchasing-power reduction does not.

Aggregate-Demand.card_intro: Build market demand by horizontally adding the quantities demanded by individual consumers at each price.
Aggregate-Demand.card_prompt: Change the number or type of consumers and add quantities at a common price.
Aggregate-Demand.intro_html: Market demand is obtained from individual demand functions by asking how much every consumer wants to buy at the same price. The operation is horizontal addition: quantities are added, not prices.
Aggregate-Demand.full_html:
Identical consumers

If each active consumer demands \(q_i(p)=10-p\), then with \(N\) identical consumers,

\[Q_D(p)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}q_i(p)=N(10-p)\]

over the range where individual demand is non-negative. Increasing \(N\) scales market quantity at every price but does not change one consumer's demand.

Heterogeneous consumers and kinks

When consumers have different demands or choke prices, include only those with positive demand at the price being considered. As price falls, additional consumers can enter the market, changing the slope of aggregate demand and creating kinks.

How to use the graph

Choose one price, read each active consumer's quantity, and add them. Repeat at several prices. This point-by-point construction is more reliable than trying to add the vertical heights of inverse-demand curves.

Check your model

Do not add quantities evaluated at different prices. Market demand answers a common-price question. Also, a change in the number of consumers shifts market demand even though no individual's preferences or income has changed.

Explore further: representative consumers

When consumers are identical, aggregate demand is a simple multiple of individual demand. With heterogeneous consumers, a single “representative” demand may hide entry thresholds, different income effects and distributional changes. Horizontal addition keeps those distinctions visible.

Consumers-Problem-HW.card_intro: Leah compares a 52% sales tax on café meals with an income tax that raises exactly the same revenue.
Consumers-Problem-HW.card_prompt: With income $702, prices $10 and $5, and u(x,y)=xy, calculate all three bundles and compare utility.
Consumers-Problem-HW.intro_html: Leah has a monthly discretionary budget of $702. She buys books \(x\) at $10 each and café meals \(y\) at $5 each. Her preferences are \(u(x,y)=xy\). The government is considering either a 52% sales tax on café meals or an income tax that raises the same revenue from Leah.
Consumers-Problem-HW.full_html:
Question

  1. Before tax, use \(I=702\), \(p_x=10\), \(p_y=5\) and \(u(x,y)=xy\) to calculate Leah's optimal bundle.
  2. A 52% sales tax raises the meal price to $7.60. Calculate Leah's new bundle and the sales-tax revenue. Then find the income-tax rate that raises the same revenue and calculate Leah's bundle under that tax.
  3. Calculate Leah's utility under the sales tax and the revenue-equivalent income tax. Which tax does she prefer, and why does the answer differ even though government revenue is the same?
Consumers-Problem-HW.answer_html:
Show the worked solution

With equal Cobb–Douglas exponents, Leah spends half of her budget on each good. Before tax,

\[(x_0,y_0)=\left(\frac{702}{2(10)},\frac{702}{2(5)}\right)=(35.1,70.2).\]

The sales-tax-inclusive meal price is \(5(1.52)=7.60\). Thus

\[(x_s,y_s)=\left(35.1,\frac{702}{2(7.6)}\right)\approx(35.1,46.184).\]

The tax collected per meal is \(0.52(5)=2.60\), so revenue is

\[R_s=2.60(46.184)\approx120.079.\]

The revenue-equivalent income-tax rate is

\[t=\frac{120.079}{702}\approx0.171053,\]

or about 17.11%. After income tax, Leah has approximately $581.921 to spend, giving

\[(x_i,y_i)\approx(29.096,58.192).\]

Utility under the sales tax is approximately \(35.1(46.184)=1621.07\). Utility under the income tax is approximately \(29.096(58.192)=1693.16\). Leah therefore prefers the revenue-equivalent income tax in this model.

The income tax leaves the relative price \(p_x/p_y\) unchanged. The sales tax makes café meals relatively more expensive and causes Leah to substitute away from \(y\). This distortion is why the equal-revenue sales tax gives lower utility.

Curves&Demand.card_intro: Link optimal choices to price-consumption curves, income-consumption curves, ordinary demand and Engel curves.
Curves&Demand.card_prompt: Switch utility types and identify which variable changes before interpreting own-price, cross-price or income responses.
Curves&Demand.intro_html: This multi-panel graph turns repeated solutions of the consumer's problem into observable demand relationships. Each curve corresponds to a different controlled experiment, so begin by naming what changes and what is held fixed.
Curves&Demand.full_html:
From choices to curves

A price-consumption curve traces optimal bundles as one price changes. Project the relevant chosen quantity against that price and obtain ordinary demand. An income-consumption curve traces optima as income changes; project quantity against income and obtain an Engel curve.

Own-price, cross-price and income responses

Own-price demand records how demand for a good changes with its own price. Cross-price demand records how demand for one good changes when the other good's price changes. An Engel curve records the income response. These are different derivatives and may have different signs.

Gross substitutes and complements

A positive cross-price response identifies gross substitutes; a negative one identifies gross complements. “Gross” means the Marshallian response combines substitution and income effects. The sign therefore cannot be read from indifference-curve curvature alone.

How to use the graph

  1. Select one preference specification.
  2. Change only one price or income.
  3. Track the new optimum in the consumption panel.
  4. Find the same observation on the projected demand or Engel curve.

Check your model

A curve traced by changing income is not a demand curve against price. Likewise, an ordinary cross-price response is not the compensated substitution effect; it also includes the purchasing-power change caused by the price movement.

Explore further: gross and net substitution

Compensated, or net, substitution holds utility fixed and isolates the relative-price response. Gross substitution uses ordinary demand and includes income effects. Two goods can therefore be compensated substitutes while appearing as gross complements for some income responses.

Curves-Expansion-Demand.card_intro: Trace optimal consumption as income or a price changes, then read the associated demand and Engel curves.
Curves-Expansion-Demand.card_prompt: Move one control at a time and connect the expansion path to its projection in the other panels.
Curves-Expansion-Demand.intro_html: The graph combines the budget line, indifference curves, demand functions and the optimal bundle. Its purpose is to show that a demand curve is not a separate assumption: it is generated by repeatedly solving the same optimisation problem under different prices or income.
Curves-Expansion-Demand.full_html:
Income expansion and Engel curves

Holding prices fixed while income changes shifts the budget line in parallel. The resulting optima trace an income-expansion path. Project a chosen quantity against income and obtain its Engel curve. An upward-sloping Engel curve indicates a normal good over that range; a downward-sloping segment indicates an inferior good.

Price consumption and ordinary demand

Changing one price rotates the budget line. The resulting optima trace a price-consumption curve. Project quantity of the price-changing good against its price and obtain ordinary own-price demand. Project the other quantity and obtain a cross-price relationship.

How to use the graph

Run separate experiments. Reset the graph, change income only, and trace the income path. Reset again, change one price only, and trace the price path. This avoids treating a movement caused by two controls as though it identified one comparative static.

Check your model

Ordinary demand includes both substitution and income effects. A downward-sloping Engel curve is evidence of inferiority only when prices are held fixed. The name of a curve comes from the experiment that generates it, not just its shape on the page.

Explore further: local classifications can change

A good can be normal over one income range and inferior over another. Likewise, cross-price responses can vary with the starting bundle. Treat “normal,” “inferior,” “gross substitute” and “gross complement” as properties of demand over a stated range, not permanent labels detached from prices and income.

Ex-2023-Q3.card_intro: Amira chooses consumption across two periods before and after a large interest-rate increase in a stylised economy.
Ex-2023-Q3.card_prompt: Calculate the initial, compensated and final bundles, then report the substitution, income and total effects.
Ex-2023-Q3.intro_html:
Amira lives for two periods and has resources \(M_1=M_2=105\). Prices are \(p_1=1\) and \(p_2=1.05\). Her preferences are

\[u(c_1,c_2)=c_1^{0.5}c_2.\]

The interest rate initially equals 5%. It then rises by 1.79, making the new rate 1.84. The large change is intentional.
Ex-2023-Q3.full_html:
Question

  1. With \(M_1=M_2=105\), \(p_1=1\), \(p_2=1.05\) and \(i=0.05\), write Amira's lifetime budget in period-2 value and calculate her initial optimal bundle.
  2. The interest rate rises to \(i'=1.84\). Calculate the new lifetime wealth, the final bundle and the total change in consumption in each period.
  3. At the new prices, calculate the compensated bundle that restores Amira's original utility. Use the initial, compensated and final bundles to calculate the substitution and income effects for both periods.
Ex-2023-Q3.answer_html:
Show the worked solution

The lifetime budget in period-2 value is

\[(1+i)p_1c_1+p_2c_2=(1+i)M_1+M_2.\]

Initially, lifetime wealth is

\[W_0=1.05(105)+105=215.25.\]

The Cobb–Douglas expenditure shares are \(1/3\) on present consumption and \(2/3\) on future consumption, so

\[(c_1^0,c_2^0)=\left(\frac{W_0}{3(1.05)},\frac{2W_0}{3(1.05)}\right)\approx(68.33,136.67).\]

After the rate rises to 1.84, the gross price is \(2.84\) and lifetime wealth is

\[W_1=2.84(105)+105=403.2.\]

The final bundle is

\[(c_1^1,c_2^1)=\left(\frac{403.2}{3(2.84)},\frac{2(403.2)}{3(1.05)}\right)\approx(47.324,256).\]

The total effects are approximately \(-21.009\) for present consumption and \(+119.333\) for future consumption.

At the new prices, the lifetime wealth needed to reach the original utility level is approximately \(W_c=299.907\). The Hicksian compensated bundle is

\[(c_1^c,c_2^c)\approx(35.200,190.417).\]

Therefore, the Hicksian substitution effects are

\[(c_1^c-c_1^0,c_2^c-c_2^0)\approx(-33.133,+53.750),\]

and the income or wealth effects are

\[(c_1^1-c_1^c,c_2^1-c_2^c)\approx(+12.124,+65.583).\]

The two components add to the total effect for each period. Amira initially saves because \(c_1^0<M_1\). The higher return raises her wealth, which explains why the income effect on present consumption is positive even though the substitution effect is negative.

IE-SE-CobbDouglas.card_intro: Decompose a price change under Cobb–Douglas preferences into substitution and income effects.
IE-SE-CobbDouglas.card_prompt: Increase the tax, construct the compensated budget and verify that both components add to the total effect.
IE-SE-CobbDouglas.intro_html: A price change does two things at once: it changes relative prices and it changes purchasing power. This graph separates those mechanisms by comparing the original optimum, a utility-compensated optimum at the new prices, and the final uncompensated optimum.
IE-SE-CobbDouglas.full_html:
Start with the three budget lines

The consumer has \(u(x,y)=xy\). A tax on good 2 changes its price from \(p_2\) to \(p_2+t\).

  • Original: \(p_1x+p_2y=I\).
  • New: \(p_1x+(p_2+t)y=I\).
  • Compensated: parallel to the new line and shifted until it reaches the original utility level.

The decomposition

Let the original, compensated and final bundles be \((x_0,y_0)\), \((x_c,y_c)\) and \((x_1,y_1)\). The original-to-compensated move is the substitution effect; the compensated-to-final move is the income effect. Coordinate by coordinate,

\[y_1-y_0=(y_c-y_0)+(y_1-y_c).\]

The same identity applies to \(x\). A positive sign means the quantity rises; a negative sign means it falls.

How to use the graph

  1. Display the original line and bundle.
  2. Turn on the taxed line and final bundle.
  3. Turn on the compensating-variation folder.
  4. If using the manual transfer, set it equal to the displayed Hicksian compensation before reading the arrows.

A worked observation from the default graph

With \(p_1=6\), \(p_2=1\), \(I=174\) and \(t=1.1\), the original bundle is \((14.5,87)\), the final bundle is approximately \((14.5,41.43)\), and the Hicksian compensated bundle is approximately \((21.01,60.04)\).

For good 2, both effects are negative. For good 1, the positive substitution effect is exactly offset by a negative income effect, so final demand returns to 14.5.

Check your model

Compensation restores the original utility, not the original bundle. At the new relative prices the consumer usually chooses a different compensated bundle. A rebate can therefore restore welfare without undoing the tax's consumption effect.

Explore further: what is special about this Cobb–Douglas example?

Demand for good 1 remains \(I/(2p_1)\) because neither income nor its own price changes. The exact cancellation of substitution and income effects is not a general property of convex preferences. Under another utility function, taxing good 2 can change final demand for good 1.

If the same proportional tax applied to both goods, their relative price would be unchanged. The tax would then create a purchasing-power effect but no substitution effect between the goods.

IE-SE-Quasilinear.display_title: Income and Substitution Effects: Quasilinear Utility
IE-SE-Quasilinear.card_intro: Use quasilinear preferences to isolate a zero income effect for one good at an interior solution.
IE-SE-Quasilinear.card_prompt: Set the compensation correctly, then compare the decompositions for x and y after the tax on good 1.
IE-SE-Quasilinear.intro_html: The graph uses \(u(x,y)=x+\sqrt y\). A unit tax on good 1 raises its effective price and rotates the budget line. Quasilinearity makes the resulting decomposition especially transparent—but only in the interior region.
IE-SE-Quasilinear.full_html:
Marshallian demand at an interior solution

The demand functions are

\[y^*=\left(\frac{p_1}{2p_2}\right)^2,\qquad x^*=\frac{I}{p_1}-\frac{p_1}{4p_2}.\]

Demand for \(y\) is independent of income. When the price of \(x\) rises, the relative-price response raises demand for \(y\).

The decomposition

At an interior solution, the income effect on \(y\) is zero, so its total response equals its substitution effect. Good \(x\) absorbs marginal income and therefore carries the purchasing-power adjustment.

How to use the graph

Display the original and taxed bundles, then set the manual transfer to the chosen Hicksian or Slutsky benchmark. Confirm that substitution plus income effect equals total effect for each coordinate. Finally lower income enough to approach a corner and observe why the interior conclusion needs a scope condition.

Check your model

A zero income effect does not mean the quantity cannot change. Demand for \(y\) responds to relative prices even though it does not respond to income in the interior. Also, without correct compensation, the graph's intermediate arrows do not isolate either economic effect.

Explore further: the corner qualification

If income is too low to afford the interior amount of \(y\), the optimum has \(x=0\). In that region, demand for \(y\) depends on income and its income effect is no longer zero. Quasilinearity simplifies local interior analysis; it does not erase the constraint.

Intertemporal-consumption.card_intro: Treat present and future consumption as two goods linked by the interest rate and lifetime resources.
Intertemporal-consumption.card_prompt: Change the interest rate or endowment and identify whether the consumer is a saver or borrower.
Intertemporal-consumption.intro_html: Intertemporal choice is a consumer problem in which the two goods are consumption at different dates. Saving transfers purchasing power into the future; borrowing transfers future resources into the present.
Intertemporal-consumption.full_html:
The lifetime budget

In future-value units,

\[(1+i)p_1c_1+p_2c_2=(1+i)M_1+M_2.\]

The slope has magnitude \((1+i)p_1/p_2\): consuming one more unit today costs both the purchase price and the return that could have been earned by saving those resources.

Saver, borrower and the endowment point

The zero-saving bundle is \((M_1/p_1,M_2/p_2)\). Choosing less period-1 consumption than the first coordinate means saving; choosing more means borrowing. An interest-rate change rotates the budget line around this endowment point.

What a higher interest rate does

A higher interest rate makes present consumption more expensive in future-consumption units, so the substitution effect moves toward future consumption. The income effect depends on the initial position: a saver receives a higher return, while a borrower faces a higher repayment cost.

How to use the graph

Before changing the rate, classify the initial choice as saving or borrowing. Then increase the rate, track the budget rotation and separate the common substitution direction from the position-dependent income effect.

Check your model

The endowment point is not necessarily the optimum. It is the bundle available without financial trade. Also, a higher interest rate need not lower present consumption for every preference and endowment because substitution and income effects can oppose each other.

Explore further: present value and future value

The same budget can be written in present-value units by dividing through by \(1+i\). The graph changes units but not the feasible set or optimum. What matters is consistency: prices, endowments and consumption must all be expressed in the same date's units.

Time-IE-SE.card_intro: Decompose an interest-rate response for smooth, kinked and corner intertemporal preferences.
Time-IE-SE.card_prompt: Choose a utility type, identify saver or borrower status, and interpret the compensated movement before the income effect.
Time-IE-SE.intro_html: An interest-rate change rotates the intertemporal budget line around the zero-saving endowment. This graph compares Cobb–Douglas, perfect-complements and perfect-substitutes preferences, showing why one decomposition method can produce very different geometry.
Time-IE-SE.full_html:
The common price change

When the interest rate rises, present consumption becomes relatively more expensive in future-value units. Whenever a smooth compensated substitution response exists, it moves away from present consumption and toward future consumption.

Why the income effect differs

A saver benefits from a higher return on transferred resources; a borrower pays more to transfer resources into the present. The income effect can therefore have different signs even when two consumers face the same new interest rate.

Kinks and corners

Perfect complements have zero Hicksian substitution effect because compensation leaves the chosen fixed-proportion kink unchanged. Perfect substitutes can jump between corners after a small price change. In both cases, forcing a smooth tangency interpretation hides the actual choice mechanism.

How to use the graph

  1. Select one utility type and record the initial endowment and choice.
  2. Classify the consumer as saver or borrower.
  3. Change the interest rate and display the correctly compensated budget.
  4. Interpret the original-to-compensated move, then the compensated-to-final move.

Check your model

If a manual transfer replaces the active compensation formula, recalibrate it before reading the arrows. A line merely parallel to the new budget is not necessarily Hicksian; it must reach the original utility level.

Explore further: why the total effect can be ambiguous

The substitution effect of a higher interest rate points away from present consumption, but a positive wealth effect for a saver can raise demand for both normal-date consumptions. If that wealth effect is strong enough, a saver may consume more today despite today's higher relative price.

Consumer-Optimization.card_intro: Connect the budget line and utility maximisation to demand, price-consumption and income-consumption curves.
Consumer-Optimization.card_prompt: Change one price or income at a time and trace how each optimum generates the corresponding relationship.
Consumer-Optimization.intro_html: This graph is a compact consumer-optimisation laboratory. It links the budget set, preferences, the chosen bundle and the demand relationships generated by repeating the problem under new prices or income.
Consumer-Optimization.full_html:
Solve the choice before reading the projection

At a smooth interior optimum, \(MRS=p_x/p_y\) and the budget binds. Those equations generate a candidate bundle. The graph then projects repeated candidates into price-consumption, income-consumption, demand and Engel curves.

Price and income experiments

A one-price change rotates the budget line and traces a price-consumption curve; plotting the relevant quantity against price gives ordinary demand. An income change shifts the line in parallel and traces an income-consumption curve; plotting quantity against income gives an Engel curve.

How to use the graph

  1. Choose a baseline and identify the current optimum.
  2. Change only one control.
  3. Explain the movement in the budget line before describing the new optimum.
  4. Locate the same choice in the demand or Engel panel.

Check your model

If a formula predicts a negative quantity or an interior point outside the budget segment, return to the original constrained problem. A first-order condition is a candidate-generating device, not permission to ignore corners, kinks or feasibility.

Explore further: demand functions carry assumptions

A closed-form demand formula usually comes from a specific preference representation and an interior-solution assumption. When parameters move far enough to create a corner, the correct demand becomes piecewise. The graph is useful for seeing exactly where the convenient formula changes regime.
